what_its_for: Thalidomide is used to treat a type of blood cancer called multiple myeloma (usually given with another medicine called dexamethasone). It is also used to treat and prevent a painful skin condition called erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), which is related to leprosy. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take thalidomide exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the capsule whole with water. You may take it with or without food, but taking it at bedtime may help reduce drowsiness during the day. Do not open, crush, or break the capsules. If a capsule breaks and the powder touches your skin, wash the area right away with soap and water. IMPORTANT: Because this medicine can cause very serious birth defects, you MUST be enrolled in a special safety program called THALOMID REMS before you can receive this medicine. Your doctor, pharmacy, and you must all follow the rules of this program.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition and other factors. For multiple myeloma, the usual dose is 200 mg once daily, often taken at bedtime. For ENL, doses typically range from 100 mg to 300 mg once daily at bedtime. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Always take it at the same time each day.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been LESS than 12 hours since your scheduled dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it has been MORE than 12 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do NOT take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store thalidomide capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the capsules in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from light and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused or expired capsules down the toilet. Ask your pharmacist about the proper way to dispose of unused medicine through a take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Do NOT donate blood while taking thalidomide and for at least 4 weeks after stopping it — donated blood could harm a pregnant woman's baby. Do NOT donate sperm while taking this medicine and for 4 weeks after stopping. Avoid drinking alcohol or taking other medicines that make you drowsy (such as sleep aids, anti-anxiety medicines, or narcotic pain medicines) unless your doctor approves, as this increases the risk of dangerous drowsiness. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Do not share this medicine with anyone else — it is illegal and extremely dangerous. Women who are pregnant or who could become pregnant must NEVER touch thalidomide capsules.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor RIGHT AWAY or go to the emergency room if you experience: numbness, tingling, burning, or pain in your hands or feet (this could be nerve damage); signs of a blood clot such as leg pain or swelling, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood; an irregular or fast heartbeat; severe skin rash or peeling skin; fever, chills, or signs of infection; unusual tiredness or weakness; dizziness or fainting; or if you think you may be pregnant. Also tell your doctor if you experience increased drowsiness, constipation, or any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: For multiple myeloma, it may take several weeks to months before you notice the full benefit of thalidomide. For ENL skin symptoms, some patients feel improvement within a few days to weeks. Keep taking your medicine as directed even if you feel well, and do not stop without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Thalidomide must NEVER be used during pregnancy. It causes life-threatening birth defects and fetal death. All women who could become pregnant must use two forms of birth control for 4 weeks before starting, throughout treatment, and for 4 weeks after stopping thalidomide. A negative pregnancy test is required before starting and regularly during treatment. BREASTFEEDING: Do not breastfeed while taking thalidomide. MALES: Men taking thalidomide must always use a condom during sexual activity with a woman who is or could become pregnant, even if they have had a vasectomy. This applies during treatment and for 4 weeks after stopping. CHILDREN: Safety in children under 12 years old has not been well established. Use with caution in children. OLDER ADULTS: Elderly patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as drowsiness, dizziness, and risk of blood clots. Report any unusual symptoms to your doctor promptly. KIDNEY or LIVER DISEASE: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as dose adjustments may be needed.
